title: ZZ v2 Pipeline Proof (delete me)
subtitle: A 17-question diagnostic for $100k-$3M/mo marketing, creative, and dev agency founders. Find which step of weekly client reporting quietly eats your team's hours, and what it costs you a year.

methodology_anchor.name: The four leak points in weekly client reporting
preconditions: Automated data pulls. Numbers flow from ad platforms, analytics, and your CRM without anyone copy-pasting cells.
A standardized template. Every client report is built on the same skeleton, so nobody rebuilds format from scratch.
Self-serve delivery. Clients can see their numbers live, so weekly deck assembly stops being the only way they get data.
A resilient approval flow. Reports go out on a rhythm without stalling on one person's sign-off.
methodology_anchor.intro: This assessment scores the four places weekly reporting hours leak: the pull, the template, the delivery, and the approval. Close all four and reporting runs itself while your team stays on the work clients pay for. Leave one open and the hours bleed back every single week.

start_screen.headline_html: See where weekly reporting hours vanish before the deck ever ships.
start_screen.description: For $100k-$3M/mo marketing, creative, and dev agency founders. Seventeen questions on how you build client reports, then a 0-100 score and the dollar cost of the manual gap.

answers.label: Boutique: $100k to $300k/mo revenue
Growing: $300k to $800k/mo revenue
Established: $800k to $1.5M/mo revenue
Scaling: $1.5M to $3M/mo revenue

questions.text: How automated is pulling numbers from ad platforms into your client reports?

answers.label: 1. Fully manual: someone logs in and copies figures each week
2. Mostly manual with a few saved views
3. Half exported, half hand-entered
4. Mostly piped in, light cleanup by hand
5. Fully automated: numbers land with zero manual entry

questions.text: How automated is pulling analytics and site data into reports?

answers.label: 1. Someone pulls screenshots or CSVs every week
2. Manual export, then reshaped by hand
3. Partly connected, partly copied
4. Connected feed, minor manual tidy
5. Live connection, no human in the pull

questions.text: How automated is pulling CRM and pipeline data into reports?

answers.label: 1. Not pulled, or typed in from memory
2. Exported and pasted each cycle
3. Some fields sync, the rest are manual
4. Mostly synced, occasional hand fix
5. Fully synced from the CRM, no touch

questions.text: How often does someone copy numbers between tools by hand to build a report?

answers.label: 1. Every report, across every metric
2. Most reports, most sections
3. About half the numbers
4. Only a few edge-case metrics
5. Never: nothing is hand-copied

low.headline: Your report is built by hand every week
low.text: Right now a person logs into three or four tools and retypes the same figures on a schedule. That is the single biggest reporting leak, and it grows with every client you sign. First fix: connect the two highest-volume sources so their numbers arrive without a login.
steps: List every source a human opens to build one report
Connect the two heaviest sources to a single sheet or warehouse first
Kill the copy-paste step for those two before touching anything else

mid.headline: Half connected, half still manual
mid.text: The easy sources flow in, but the awkward ones still get hand-entered, and that is where errors and late nights live. What I'd do: attack the last manual source instead of polishing the ones that already work.
steps: Find the one source that still forces a manual pull
Connect it or replace it with a tool that has an API
Set the whole pull to refresh on a schedule, not on request

high.headline: The pull runs itself
high.text: Data lands with no human in the loop. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add a freshness check that flags a broken feed before a client sees stale numbers
Log which source breaks most and harden it
Reuse the same pipeline for internal dashboards, not just client reports

operator_brief.headline_number: recoverable hours: high. Manual multi-source pulls are the top-quartile reporting leak for agencies this size.
operator_brief.lever: My read: connect the two heaviest data sources first and delete their copy-paste step before touching template or design.
talking_points: Every source we open by hand is a weekly tax that scales with client count.
Automating the pull removes the error risk of retyping numbers under deadline.
One connected pipeline serves both client reports and our own dashboards.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: In one week, wire a single client's ad and analytics data into one sheet that refreshes on a schedule, then time the report build before and after.

questions.text: How standardized is your report template across all clients?

answers.label: 1. Every client report is built from scratch
2. A loose starting point, heavily customized each time
3. A shared template that drifts per client
4. One template with a few approved variants
5. One locked template, swap the data and go

questions.text: How consistent are your metric definitions from client to client?

answers.label: 1. Each report defines metrics differently
2. Mostly ad hoc, decided by whoever builds it
3. Some agreed, some improvised
4. A documented set, minor exceptions
5. One definition library, applied everywhere

questions.text: How often does report format get rebuilt or reinvented per client?

answers.label: 1. Constantly: layout is redone almost every time
2. Often, whenever a client asks for something new
3. Sometimes, for larger accounts
4. Rarely, the format is mostly fixed
5. Never: format is locked and reused

low.headline: Every report is a custom build
low.text: With no shared template, each report reinvents layout, metrics, and structure, so the work never gets faster no matter how many you ship. First fix: freeze one template from your best existing report and force the next five clients onto it.
steps: Pick your cleanest current report as the master
Strip client-specific bits into a swappable data block
Roll the next five clients onto the frozen template

mid.headline: A template exists but it drifts
mid.text: You started with structure, then let each client pull it in a new direction, so you now maintain many near-copies. What I'd do: collapse the variants back to one template with a short list of approved options.
steps: Audit how many template versions are live right now
Merge them into one core plus two or three approved add-ons
Write a one-page rule for when a variant is allowed

high.headline: One template, swap and ship
high.text: Format and metrics are locked and reused. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Version the template so improvements roll to every client at once
Add a metric definition library the whole team references
Templatize the written insight section, not only the charts

operator_brief.headline_number: recoverable hours: medium to high. Rebuilding layout per client is a repeated cost that compounds with headcount.
operator_brief.lever: What I'd do: freeze one master template and treat any per-client format change as an exception that needs a reason.
talking_points: A single template means a new hire ships a correct report on day one.
Consistent metric definitions stop clients arguing about numbers that mean different things.
Improving one template upgrades every client report at once.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Take last week's messiest report, rebuild it once as a locked template, and build next week's from it to measure the time drop.

questions.text: Total hours your team spends per week building client reports by hand?
questions.hint: Add up everyone who touches reporting, across every client, in a normal week.

questions.text: Average loaded hourly cost per person doing this reporting?
questions.hint: Salary plus overhead divided by working hours. Used to price the manual gap. A rough figure is fine.

questions.text: How many people touch the reporting process in a given week?
questions.hint: Everyone who pulls, builds, reviews, or approves a client report.

questions.text: How predictable is the weekly time your team loses to reporting?

answers.label: 1. It swallows whatever time it wants, every week
2. Usually a scramble near deadline
3. Roughly known, but it slips often
4. Fairly steady and boxed in
5. Fixed and small: reporting is a rounding error

low.headline: Reporting is eating real payroll
low.text: The hours you entered turn into a number your team feels every week and your P and L feels every year. When many people touch each report, coordination adds cost on top of the raw hours. First fix: cut the manual pull, because that is the step that scales worst with client count.
steps: Look at your weekly and annual leak figures on the results screen
Attribute the hours to pull, build, or approval
Automate the largest bucket first and re-measure in two weeks

mid.headline: The load is known but still heavy
mid.text: You have a sense of the cost, and it is not trivial. What I'd do: shrink the number of people who touch a report, since every extra handoff adds time and a chance to introduce an error.
steps: Map who does what on a single report end to end
Collapse two handoffs into one owner where you can
Reinvest the recovered hours into client-facing work, not more reports

high.headline: Reporting barely registers on the clock
high.text: Hours are low and predictable. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Track reporting hours as a metric so drift shows early
Pressure-test what happens to the number when you double clients
Redeploy the saved capacity into strategy the client will pay more for

operator_brief.headline_number: Weekly leak = reporting_hours x loaded hourly rate. Annual = that figure x 52 weeks. Both computed live from your inputs on the results screen.
operator_brief.lever: Honest take: the fastest dollar recovery is removing the manual pull, because it is the hours line that grows every time you add a retainer.
talking_points: Our own numbers put a dollar figure on manual reporting, not a guess.
Fewer hands on each report cuts both cost and error rate.
Recovered hours can move to work clients actually pay a premium for.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: For one week, log actual reporting hours per person, multiply by loaded rate, and bring the annualized figure to your next leadership check-in.

questions.text: How often do clients get real-time dashboards instead of static weekly decks?

answers.label: 1. Always a static deck, built and sent by hand
2. Mostly decks, a dashboard for one or two clients
3. Split between dashboards and decks
4. Mostly live dashboards, deck on request
5. Every client has a live dashboard by default

questions.text: How self-serve is client access to their own numbers between reports?

answers.label: 1. They only see numbers when we send them
2. They can ask, and we pull on demand
3. A few have a link, most do not
4. Most can log in and check anytime
5. All clients self-serve, no ad hoc pulls

questions.text: How much of report time goes to insight and narrative versus assembling data?

answers.label: 1. Nearly all time is spent assembling data
2. Mostly assembly, a little analysis
3. Even split
4. Mostly analysis, assembly is quick
5. Almost all time is insight: data assembles itself

low.headline: Clients only see numbers when you hand-deliver them
low.text: Static decks built by a person are the most expensive way to show a client their data, and they leave your team as the only path to a number. First fix: stand up one live dashboard for a friendly client and let them watch it instead of waiting for a deck.
steps: Pick one client comfortable with a live view
Connect the data you already pull into a shared dashboard
Shift that account to a short narrative on top of the live link

mid.headline: Some live, most still hand-sent
mid.text: A couple of clients self-serve while the rest wait on a deck, which keeps your team assembling instead of advising. What I'd do: move the next tier of clients to dashboards so your hours go to insight, which is the part they actually value.
steps: Rank clients by how much deck-building they trigger
Roll dashboards to the top three time sinks next
Rewrite the weekly touch as a short read on the numbers, not a rebuild

high.headline: Clients self-serve, you advise
high.text: Data is live and your time goes to narrative. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add alerting so clients hear from you when a number moves, not on a calendar
Template the insight layer so analysis stays fast
Use the dashboard as a retention and upsell surface, not just reporting

operator_brief.headline_number: recoverable hours: medium. Static deck assembly is a repeat weekly cost that a live dashboard removes once.
operator_brief.lever: My read: put clients on a live view so your team spends its hours on the insight clients pay for, not on rebuilding charts.
talking_points: A live dashboard turns a weekly build into a one-time setup.
Self-serve access makes us the interpreter of the numbers, a higher-value seat.
Insight time is billable value, assembly time is pure cost.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: Stand up one shared dashboard for a single client this week and replace their next deck with a five-line written read on the live numbers.

questions.text: How often do reports stall on one person's approval before they go out?

answers.label: 1. Everything waits on one person, always
2. Most reports need that one sign-off
3. Larger accounts bottleneck, others flow
4. Rarely: approval is quick and shared
5. Never: reports ship on a rule, not a person

questions.text: How well does reporting hold up when the key person is out?

answers.label: 1. It stops: nobody else can build or send
2. It slips badly until they return
3. It limps along with errors
4. It mostly runs, minor gaps
5. It runs identically whether they are in or out

questions.text: How documented is your end-to-end reporting process?

answers.label: 1. Nothing written: it lives in one head
2. A few scattered notes
3. Partly documented, often stale
4. Mostly documented and current
5. Fully documented, anyone can run it

low.headline: Reporting lives in one person's head
low.text: When one person approves and only they know the process, every report is one sick day away from a missed deadline. First fix: write the process down and set a clear rule for what ships without a manual sign-off.
steps: Have the key person narrate one full report build as you document it
Define which reports can ship on a rule with no approval
Name a backup who can run the process from the doc

mid.headline: The bottleneck shows up on your biggest accounts
mid.text: Most reports flow, but the accounts that matter most still queue behind one approver. What I'd do: move approval from a person to a checklist so the report clears itself when it meets the bar.
steps: Turn the approver's mental checks into a written checklist
Let a report auto-clear when the checklist passes
Reserve the human review for exceptions and new clients only

high.headline: Reports ship on a rule, not a person
high.text: Approval is fast and the process is documented. Keep sharpening. Here is the frontier.
steps: Add a light audit trail so you can trace any number a client questions
Review the checklist quarterly so it does not go stale
Cross-train a second owner so resilience never regresses

operator_brief.headline_number: risk band: high when one person owns both the build and the sign-off. This is a single point of failure, not just a time cost.
operator_brief.lever: Honest take: convert approval into a written checklist so reports clear on meeting a bar, not on catching one person's attention.
talking_points: A documented process removes the key-person risk on client deliverables.
A checklist-based sign-off scales without adding review hours.
Resilience here protects renewals: missed reports read as neglect to a client.
operator_brief.proof_of_concept: This week, document one full report build and let a teammate ship the next report from that doc alone, with the usual approver only watching.

computed_outputs.label: Est. weekly cost of manual reporting
Est. annual cost of the manual reporting gap (52 weeks)

tier_boutique.closing: At $100k to $300k/mo you are likely doing reporting yourself or leaning on one or two people, so every manual hour comes straight off your own week. The leaks are real, but a full reporting build has a longer payback at your scale. Fix the single worst pull by hand first, and revisit the rest once headcount grows.
tier_boutique.proof: The pattern I'd watch for at your size: reporting stays cheap until you cross roughly ten retainers, then the manual pull turns into a weekly fire. Getting ahead of it before that break point is the cheap move.
tier_boutique.cta_description: Follow the weekly teardowns and retake this when you cross into the next revenue tier.

tier_growing.closing: At $300k to $800k/mo you have enough clients that manual reporting is now a scheduled tax on a growing team, and it is probably the least visible cost on your books. This is the tier where automating the pull pays back fastest, because the hours you save compound with every new retainer you sign.
tier_growing.proof: The pattern I'd watch for: agencies your size often carry a reporting load that would fund most of a junior hire, hidden across a few people's calendars. Your annual leak figure on the results screen makes that visible.
tier_growing.cta_description: I'll review your exact answers against agencies your size and send back the one reporting fix I'd prioritize first.

tier_established.closing: At $800k to $1.5M/mo, reporting touches enough hands that coordination itself is now a cost, and a single approver bottleneck can quietly cap how many accounts you deliver well. The move at your tier is turning reporting from a person-dependent scramble into a documented, mostly automated system.
tier_established.proof: The pattern I'd watch for: at your size the biggest risk is not the raw hours, it is that your best accounts queue behind one person's sign-off. That is a renewal risk dressed up as a workflow quirk.
tier_established.cta_description: I'll stack your answers against agencies your size and send a Loom on the highest-leverage reporting fix for a team your scale.

tier_scaling.closing: At $1.5M to $3M/mo, small per-report inefficiencies multiply across a large client base into a serious line of cost and risk. At this tier the question is no longer whether to automate reporting, it is whether the system is resilient enough to survive people leaving and clients doubling.
tier_scaling.proof: The pattern I'd watch for: agencies your size that still hand-build reports are usually one departure away from a delivery gap. Systematizing the pull, template, and approval is what protects margin at scale.
tier_scaling.cta_description: I'll review your answers against agencies at your scale and send a Loom on the reporting fix with the biggest margin and risk impact.
